'''Matzah balls''' or '''matzo balls''' are [[Ashkenazi Jew]]ish soup morsels made from a mixture of [[matzah meal]], beaten eggs, water, and a fat, such as oil, [[margarine]], or [[schmaltz|chicken fat]]. Known as '''knaidel''' in [[Yiddish]] ({{langx|yi|קניידלעך|kneydlekh}} pl., singular {{langx|yi|קניידל|kneydl|label=none}}; with numerous other transliterations), they resemble a matzah meal version of [[Knödel]], bread dumplings popular throughout [[Central European cuisine|Central European]] and [[East European cuisine]].<ref name="The New York Times 2006 s203">{{cite web | title=Ghosts of Passovers Past | website=The New York Times | date=2006-04-09 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/04/09/magazine/09food.html | quote=You would think it would be easy to pull together a Seder in Berlin, since many typically Jewish foods are mainstream German fare too: potato pancakes with applesauce, poppy-seed cake, rye bread. Sauerbraten looks and tastes a lot like brisket. Even matzo balls bear a striking resemblance to Knödel, starchy balls that are usually served as a side dish with gravy. But the devil is in the details. Knödel, for instance, are made with bread. | access-date=16 September 2023 | archive-date=18 September 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230918045709/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/04/09/magazine/09food.html | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Glazer Glazer 2011 p. 21">{{cite book | last1=Glazer | first1=P. | last2=Glazer | first2=M. | title=The Essential Book of Jewish Festival Cooking: 200 Seasonal Holiday Recipes and Their Traditions | publisher=HarperCollins | year=2011 | isbn=978-0-06-204121-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VMUScUO5XagC&pg=PA21 | access-date=2023-09-16 | page=21|quote= Once asked on a radio show about the derivation of knaidlach, I explained that the original knaidlach were actually rock hard, and created by Azhkenazic housewives as a weapon of self-defence… The real origin of the knaidel, according to author John Cooper, is the south German Knödel, or dumpling—popular in German cuisine since the Middle Ages.}}</ref><ref name="Cooper 1993">{{cite book | last=Cooper | first=John | title=Eat and be Satisfied: A Social History of Jewish Food | publisher=Jason Aronson | series=G - Reference, Information and Interdisciplinary Subjects Series | year=1993 | isbn=978-0-87668-316-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ld7fuK6peH8C |page=155}}</ref>

Matzah balls are traditionally served in [[chicken soup]] and are a staple food on the Jewish holiday of [[Passover]]. However, they are not eaten during Passover by those who observe [[gebrochts|a prohibition on soaking matzah products]].

The texture of matzah balls may be light or dense, depending on the recipe. Matzah balls made from some recipes float in soup; others sink.<ref name="Roman, Alison">{{cite web |author=Roman, Alison |title=How to Master Matzo Ball Soup |url=http://www.bonappetit.com/recipes/article/matzo-ball-soup |work=Bon Appetit |date=2 April 2014 |access-date=9 April 2014 |archive-date=22 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231122232353/https://www.bonappetit.com/recipes/article/matzo-ball-soup |url-status=live }}</ref>
